course.name: VIBE 101: Vibe Coding 101
course.syllabus_body:
VIBE 101: Vibe Coding 101

Introduction to Building Software with AI Assistants
Credits 3
Term Autumn (14 weeks)
Instructor Dr. Quinn Ferrous
TAs Maya Okafor, Dev Raman
Lecture Tue/Thu 11:10–12:30
Office hours Wed 2–4 PM, or by appointment ("the vibe is immaculate" is not an appointment request)
Prerequisites One prior programming course (any language)
Textbook Vibes, Prompts, and Production: A Field Guide to Vibe Coding (provided in course materials)

Course Description

Vibe coding is the practice of building software by describing what you want to an AI assistant, then steering, testing, and fixing what comes back. It is fast, fun, and occasionally catastrophic. This course teaches you to do it well: writing clear specifications, reading code you did not write, testing before trusting, and shipping something that still works on Monday.

You will not be graded on how much code the AI wrote. You will be graded on whether you understand it, can defend it, and can fix it when it breaks. The AI is your pair programmer, not your lawyer.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

  1. Explain what vibe coding is, where it works well, and where it fails, including its effect on speed, quality, and maintainability.
  2. Write precise prompts and specifications that include requirements, constraints, inputs/outputs, and examples.
  3. Read and critique AI-generated code for correctness, clarity, efficiency, and style.
  4. Test and debug AI-generated code using unit tests, edge cases, and systematic debugging rather than re-rolling the prompt and hoping.
  5. Identify and mitigate security, privacy, and licensing risks in AI-assisted development.
  6. Iterate and document a development process, including a prompt log and decision record, to build and ship a small working application.
  7. Evaluate when to use AI assistance and when to write code by hand, and justify that decision.

Weekly Schedule

Week Topic Reading Due
1 What Is Vibe Coding? Ch. 1
2 Prompting as Specification Ch. 2 Assignment 1 assigned
3 Specs, Examples, and Constraints Ch. 2 Quiz 1
4 Reading Code You Didn't Write Ch. 3 Assignment 1 due
5 Code Review for Humans (and Robots) Ch. 3 Assignment 2 assigned
6 Tests First, Vibes Second Ch. 4 Quiz 2
7 Debugging AI Code Ch. 4 Assignment 2 due
8 Midterm Exam Ch. 1–4 Midterm
9 Security and Secrets Ch. 5 Assignment 3 assigned
10 Licensing, Privacy, and Ethics Ch. 5 Quiz 3
11 Agents, Tools, and Automation Ch. 6 Assignment 3 due
12 Project Studio Final project proposal
13 Project Studio / Demos Final project draft
14 Demo Day and Review Final project due
Finals Final Exam Ch. 1–6 Final

Grading

Component Weight
Assignments (3) 30%
Final Project 10%
Quizzes (3, lowest score dropped) 15%
Midterm Exam 15%
Final Exam 20%
Participation and Prompt Logs 10%

Scale: A 93.00-99.99 | A- 90.00-92.99 | B+ 87.00-89.99 | B 83.00-86.99 | B- 80.00-82.99 | C+ 77.00-79.99 | C 73.00-76.99 | C- 70.00-72.99 | D 60.00-69.99 | E below 60.00

AI Use Policy

This is a course about using AI, so you are expected to use it. The rules:

  • Always allowed: AI assistants for assignments and the final project, with a prompt log submitted alongside your work.
  • Never allowed: submitting code you cannot explain. If the TA asks you what line 42 does and the answer is "the AI wrote that," you will receive a gentle but firm zero on that line.
  • Exams: closed AI. You will be asked to read, trace, and write code by hand. Bring a pencil and your own brain.
  • Fabrication: inventing prompt logs, fake test results, or "I tested this" when you did not is an academic integrity violation.

Late Policy

  • Assignments lose 10% per day, up to 3 days. After that, they are not accepted.
  • Two free "grace days" are available for the semester. No explanation needed.
  • Documented emergencies and accommodations are handled case by case. Email the instructor early.

Academic Integrity

Collaboration on concepts is encouraged. Collaboration on code must be disclosed in your submission. Copying another student's work or their prompt log is not permitted. When in doubt, disclose.

Accessibility and Accommodations

Students with documented accommodations should contact the instructor within the first two weeks. All course materials are provided in screen-reader-friendly formats.

Well-Being

Debugging at 2 AM is a rite of passage, but sleep is also a feature. If you are struggling, reach out to the instructor, a TA, or your campus counseling services.

pages.title: Textbook: A Field Guide to Vibe Coding
pages.body: "The code compiles. The vibes are good. What could go wrong?" — Famous last words, every semester

pages.title: Textbook Chapter 1: What Is Vibe Coding?
pages.body:
1.1 Definition

Vibe coding is a style of software development in which the programmer describes intent in natural language and relies on an AI assistant to generate most of the code. The programmer's job shifts from typing to directing, reviewing, and verifying.

1.2 A Short History

Programming has always moved toward higher abstraction: machine code, assembly, compilers, high-level languages, frameworks. Vibe coding is the next step in that sequence. The difference is that earlier abstractions were deterministic. A compiler given the same input produces the same output. A language model does not. That single fact explains most of this book.

1.3 Where It Works

  • Prototypes and throwaway scripts
  • Boilerplate (config files, CRUD endpoints, data parsing)
  • Learning a new library or language
  • Translating code between languages
  • Writing first drafts of tests

1.4 Where It Struggles

  • Large codebases with unwritten conventions
  • Performance-critical or safety-critical code
  • Novel algorithms with no good public examples
  • Anything where "mostly right" is not good enough

1.5 The Vibe Coding Loop

  1. Describe what you want.
  2. Generate code with the assistant.
  3. Read what came back.
  4. Test it.
  5. Refine the prompt, the code, or both.

Skipping step 3 or 4 is how you end up deploying a login page that accepts any password. This has happened. Not in this class, but somewhere.

1.6 Key Idea: You Own the Output

The assistant writes the code. You ship it. If it breaks production, "the AI did it" is not a defense, in the same way "autocomplete did it" never was.

1.7 The Programmer's New Work

Vibe coding changes which parts of programming take the most time. The assistant can draft syntax quickly, but it cannot decide what a product should do unless a person explains the need. The programmer still has to:

  • Find out what the user actually needs.
  • Turn that need into rules the software can follow.
  • Decide which parts of the codebase are safe to change.
  • Check the result against examples and real constraints.
  • Explain and maintain the code after the conversation ends.

For example, "add a search box" leaves important questions unanswered. Should the search match partial words? Is it case-sensitive? Should it search archived items? What should appear when there are no results? The model can choose defaults, but those choices become product behavior. A useful developer makes the choices explicit or asks the user before guessing.

1.8 Choose the Right Size of Task

AI work is easier to review when each request has a clear boundary. "Build the whole store" combines product decisions, page design, data storage, payments, and security. A smaller task such as "add a sort control to the existing product list; keep the current filters and add a test for ascending price order" has a visible result and a way to check it.

Before delegating, identify the expected change, the files or behavior that should stay stable, and how you will recognize success. If those are hard to state, spend time clarifying the problem first.

1.9 A Practical Decision Rule

Use an assistant when it can save drafting time and you can review the result. For unfamiliar code, consequential decisions, or high-risk behavior, reduce the task size and ask for explanation alongside the change. Do not delegate a decision simply because the code is easy to generate. A generated answer is useful only when a person can judge whether it is correct.

pages.title: Textbook Chapter 2: Prompting as Specification
pages.body:
2.1 A Prompt Is a Spec

A vague prompt produces vague code. Compare:

Weak: "Make a to-do app."

Strong: "Write a Python command-line to-do app. Commands: add <text>, done <id>, list. Store tasks in a JSON file tasks.json. IDs are integers starting at 1 and never reused. list prints [ ] 1 Buy milk or [x] 1 Buy milk. Use only the standard library."

The second prompt names the language, interface, storage, ID rules, output format, and constraints.

2.2 The Five Parts of a Good Prompt

  1. Goal: what the code should do
  2. Context: language, framework, existing code
  3. Constraints: libraries allowed, style, performance, what not to do
  4. Examples: sample inputs and expected outputs
  5. Format: how you want the answer (full file, diff, explanation)

2.3 Examples Beat Adjectives

"Make it robust" means nothing. "Return None if the list is empty; raise ValueError if any element is negative" means something. Give edge cases explicitly.

2.4 Iterating Without Spiraling

When the output is wrong, resist re-rolling. Instead:

  • Identify what is wrong (wrong behavior, wrong style, wrong approach).
  • Tell the assistant specifically.
  • Change one thing at a time.

If you have rewritten the same prompt six times with minor tweaks, the problem is probably your spec, not the model.

2.5 Prompt Logs

A prompt log records your prompts, the assistant's key responses, and what you changed. It documents your process and lets others (and future you) understand why the code looks the way it does.

2.6 Add Context That Changes the Answer

Context is useful when it narrows the solution. Include the relevant language and version, the framework, nearby function signatures, data shapes, and project conventions. For a change inside an existing project, point the assistant to the files it should inspect instead of asking it to invent a new structure.

Avoid dumping unrelated files or secrets into a prompt. More text is not automatically more context: details that do not affect the requirement can distract from the important constraints. Share the smallest safe example that still shows the problem.

2.7 State Boundaries and Failure Behavior

A complete spec describes what happens when the ordinary path does not work. For a file import, say what to do if the file is missing, a row is malformed, or a required field is blank. For an API endpoint, say which status code represents invalid input and whether a failed request may have changed data.

Also state boundaries on the assistant's work. For example: "Use the existing database layer. Do not add dependencies. Do not change the response schema. If the schema cannot support this behavior, explain the limitation before editing." This makes a proposed change easier to review and reduces accidental scope growth.

2.8 Example: Turn a Feature Request into a Spec

Suppose the request is "let me filter tasks by status." A reviewable prompt could be:

In the existing task list, add a status filter with All, Open, and Done choices. Keep the current sort order and task actions. The selected filter should remain active after marking a task done. If there are no matching tasks, show "No tasks in this view." Use the current UI components and do not add a package. Add or update tests for each filter choice and the empty state. First inspect the task list and report which files you plan to change.

This prompt defines the choices, interaction with existing behavior, empty state, technical constraints, and a first checkpoint. It still leaves room for implementation, while making the expected result concrete.

2.9 Review the Plan Before the Patch

For work spanning several files, ask for a short plan before code is changed. Check whether the plan touches the right parts of the application and preserves existing behavior. Correct the plan early if it assumes a new dependency, changes an unrelated interface, or misses an edge case. For a one-line change, the extra planning step may not be useful; match the process to the size and risk of the task.

pages.title: Textbook Chapter 3: Reading Code You Didn't Write
pages.body:
3.1 Why Reading Matters More Now

When you write code yourself, you understand it by default. When an assistant writes it, understanding is a separate step that you must do deliberately.

3.2 A Reading Checklist

  1. Does it match the spec? Check each requirement.
  2. Trace it by hand on a small example.
  3. Check boundaries: empty input, single element, maximum size, negative numbers, None/null.
  4. Check hidden assumptions: is it assuming sorted input? Unique elements? Specific encodings?
  5. Check dependencies: does it import a library that exists? (Assistants sometimes invent them.)
  6. Look for smells: unused variables, duplicated logic, swallowed exceptions, magic numbers.

3.3 Common AI Code Failure Modes

  • Hallucinated APIs: calls to functions or packages that do not exist.
  • Plausible but wrong logic: off-by-one errors, wrong comparison operators.
  • Silent error handling: a bare except: pass that hides every failure.
  • Mutable default arguments: def f(x, items=[]) in Python shares one list across calls.
  • Outdated practices: deprecated functions, old library versions.
  • Overengineering: a factory pattern for a 10-line script.

3.4 Example

def average(nums):
    return sum(nums) / len(nums)

Looks fine. But average([]) raises ZeroDivisionError. Is that acceptable? Only if the spec says so. Otherwise, it is a bug.

3.5 Trace Data, Not Just Lines

To understand a function, follow one concrete input from its first line to its return value. Write down the values that matter after each step. For average([2, 4, 6]), sum(nums) is 12, len(nums) is 3, and the result is 4.0 in Python. Then trace an empty list. The length is zero, so the division fails. This small trace exposes both the intended calculation and an unhandled boundary.

For a larger function, follow the data across calls: where does an input come from, which checks run, what gets changed, and what is returned or displayed? Names can be misleading. The actual values and control flow show what the program does.

3.6 Follow the Data Across Trust Boundaries

Code that handles user input, files, network responses, or database rows deserves extra attention. Ask:

  • Where was this value created, and can the user control it?
  • Is it checked before it is used in a query, file path, command, or HTML page?
  • Is sensitive information logged or returned in an error?
  • Does the code assume a network response always has the expected shape?

For example, inserting a search term directly into SQL can let punctuation change the query itself. Parameterized queries keep the search term as data. Similarly, escaping text before putting it into HTML prevents text like <script> from being treated as markup. Look for the protection at the place where the value crosses into the new context.

3.7 Read Dependencies and Side Effects

An unfamiliar function may write a file, update a database, send a request, or mutate an object even if its name sounds harmless. Inspect the functions it calls and the libraries they come from. Check whether an operation can be repeated safely. A retry of a read is usually harmless; a retry of "charge this card" can create a second charge unless the operation is designed to be idempotent.

Check dependency names and APIs against the project's installed version or official documentation. A plausible import is not proof that a package exists, and an API remembered from another version may have different behavior. Keep dependencies limited to what the project needs.

3.8 Use a Review Pass

After tracing, compare the implementation against the spec one requirement at a time. Look at the changed lines and their surrounding code, then ask:

  1. Does each requirement have a corresponding behavior or test?
  2. Did the change alter any behavior that was supposed to stay stable?
  3. Are errors visible and useful, or swallowed?
  4. Are names and control flow understandable to the next person?
  5. Can I explain why each changed line is needed?

If you cannot explain a section, ask for an explanation or simplify it before accepting the change. Reading code is not a formality; it is how you take ownership of the result.

pages.title: Textbook Chapter 4: Tests First, Vibes Second
pages.body:
4.1 Why Tests Are the Seatbelt

Tests turn "it seems to work" into "it works on these cases." With AI-generated code, tests are your main defense against confident nonsense.

4.2 Test-First Prompting

  1. Write the spec.
  2. Write tests (by hand, or ask the assistant and then review them).
  3. Ask the assistant to write code that passes the tests.
  4. Run the tests.

Note that AI-written tests for AI-written code can share the same blind spots. Review both.

4.3 What to Test

  • Normal cases: typical inputs
  • Edge cases: empty, one item, very large, duplicates
  • Error cases: invalid input, missing files
  • Regression cases: every bug you fix gets a test so it stays fixed

4.4 A Minimal Example

def test_average_basic():
    assert average([2, 4, 6]) == 4

def test_average_empty():
    # spec: return 0 for empty list
    assert average([]) == 0

4.5 Systematic Debugging

When something fails:

  1. Reproduce it with the smallest input possible.
  2. Locate where actual behavior diverges from expected (print statements, debugger, tracing).
  3. Hypothesize a cause.
  4. Fix one thing.
  5. Re-run all tests.

Do not paste the error into the assistant and accept the first fix without reading it. Sometimes the "fix" is deleting the test.

4.6 Turn Requirements into Test Cases

Each requirement should lead to at least one observable check. If a function promises to sort numbers from low to high, a useful test checks the returned order. If it promises not to change the input list, a second assertion checks that the original list is unchanged. If it promises to reject invalid values, test that it rejects them in the documented way.

For a parse_age function, a small test table might include:

Input Expected result
"18" integer 18
"0" integer 0
"eighteen" a clear validation error
"-1" a clear validation error
" 18 " follow the spec: accept trimmed input or reject it

The last row is useful because it exposes a decision the spec must make. A test should record the intended behavior, not silently invent it.

4.7 Unit, Integration, and End-to-End Checks

Different tests answer different questions:

  • Unit tests check a small function or component in isolation. They are quick and help pinpoint logic errors.
  • Integration tests check that parts work together, such as an API route saving data through the database layer.
  • End-to-end tests exercise a user path through the running application, such as signing in and submitting a form.

Use the smallest test type that can catch the risk you care about. A unit test can prove that a validator rejects a blank name, but it cannot prove that the web form actually calls the validator. An end-to-end test can check that path, but usually takes longer and gives less precise failure information.

4.8 Read the Failure Before Changing Code

A failed test gives evidence, not a diagnosis. Read the expected value, actual value, input, and stack trace. Find the first line in your code where behavior diverges. Then state a hypothesis before editing, such as "the filter compares uppercase input to lowercase labels." This keeps debugging focused and makes it easier to tell whether the fix addressed the cause.

When asking an assistant to help, include the smallest relevant code and the complete failure output, but remove secrets and personal data. Ask it to explain the likely cause and suggest a narrow fix. Review that suggestion against the evidence; do not weaken a valid test just to get a green result.

4.9 Keep Tests Trustworthy

Tests are software too. A test can pass for the wrong reason if it checks only that a function returned something, mocks away the behavior under review, or repeats the same mistaken assumption as the implementation. Prefer assertions that express the requirement directly. Include a negative case when errors matter, and keep test data small enough that a person can inspect it.

After fixing a defect, keep a regression test that fails on the old behavior and passes on the new one. Run the relevant test first, then the broader suite needed to catch nearby regressions. Report which checks ran and any that remain unverified.

pages.title: Textbook Chapter 5: Security, Privacy, and Ethics
pages.body:
5.1 Secrets

Never paste API keys, passwords, or private data into a prompt. Never commit them to a repository. Use environment variables and .gitignore. Assistants will cheerfully generate code with API_KEY = "sk-12345" hard-coded. Do not keep it.

5.2 Common Vulnerabilities in Generated Code

  • SQL injection: building queries with string concatenation instead of parameterized queries.
  • Missing input validation: trusting user input.
  • Insecure defaults: debug mode on, wide-open CORS, weak password hashing.
  • Dependency risk: installing packages that are abandoned, malicious, or non-existent ("slopsquatting").

5.3 Privacy

Do not send other people's personal data to a third-party assistant unless you are permitted to. Know where your data goes and how the tool's provider uses it.

5.4 Licensing

Generated code may resemble existing open-source code. Check your tool's policies and your project's license requirements. When in doubt, cite, rewrite, or choose a different approach.

5.5 Ethics and Responsibility

You are accountable for what you ship. Consider who might be harmed by errors, bias, or misuse, and be honest with users and teammates about what was AI-assisted.

5.6 Treat Every Input as Untrusted

Input validation and output encoding solve different problems. Validation checks whether a value fits the application's rules: a quantity might need to be a positive integer within an allowed limit. Encoding makes a value safe for the context where it is used: HTML text must be escaped as HTML, and SQL values should be passed as parameters rather than joined into a query string.

Do not rely on a browser form or a user interface to enforce rules. A caller can send a request directly. Enforce important rules on the server at the point where the data enters the system, and repeat checks where they protect a sensitive operation.

5.7 Review Authentication and Authorization Separately

Authentication asks "who is making this request?" Authorization asks "is this person allowed to perform this action on this object?" A login check alone does not prevent one user from reading another user's record. For every endpoint that reads or changes private data, identify the owner or role check and verify it uses the requested object's identity, not a value supplied by the client without validation.

Ask the assistant to explain where each check happens. Then inspect the code path yourself, including error paths. Tests should cover both an authorized request and a request from someone who should be denied.

5.8 Handle Secrets and Sensitive Data Deliberately

Keep secrets in environment variables or an approved secret store, and make sure local secret files are excluded from version control. A secret should not appear in source code, test output, screenshots, error messages, or prompt logs. If a key is exposed, removing it from a file is not enough; revoke or rotate it because old copies may remain in history or logs.

Before sharing a bug report with an assistant, replace names, account numbers, tokens, and private records with representative fake values. Preserve the shape of the data so the example remains useful without disclosing the original.

5.9 Check Dependencies and Generated Commands

An assistant may recommend a package with a familiar name that is misspelled, abandoned, or controlled by an unrelated publisher. Verify the exact package, maintainer, version, license, and project activity using the package registry and official documentation. Prefer existing dependencies when they already solve the problem.

Read installation and shell commands before running them. Understand what files they change, what data they send, and whether they delete or overwrite anything. Avoid piping a downloaded script directly into a shell. For database migrations or destructive commands, inspect the target and make a recoverable backup before execution.

5.10 Make Risk Proportional to Review

The higher the impact of an error, the stronger the review should be. A formatting helper may need a focused test and code review. A change to payment processing, medical records, access control, or data deletion needs a threat review, careful tests, and an experienced human reviewer. If the team cannot explain the generated logic or validate its assumptions, do not ship it into a high-impact path.

pages.title: Textbook Chapter 6: Agents, Tools, and Automation
pages.body:
6.1 From Chat to Agents

Early assistants answered questions. Modern ones can run commands, edit files, and call tools. An agent is an assistant that takes multiple steps toward a goal with some autonomy.

6.2 Benefits and Risks

Benefits: faster multi-file changes, automated test-fix loops, less copy-pasting. Risks: unintended file changes, runaway costs, deleted data, actions you did not approve.

6.3 Guardrails

  • Work in a version-controlled repository so every change can be reverted.
  • Give the agent the minimum permissions it needs.
  • Require approval for destructive or irreversible actions.
  • Review the diff before accepting changes.
  • Keep a human checkpoint before anything reaches production.

6.4 When Not to Use AI

Use your own hands when the code is security-critical and you need full understanding, when you are learning a concept and need the struggle, or when the cost of a mistake is high and review time exceeds writing time.

6.5 Give an Agent a Bounded Job

An agent works best when its task has a clear goal, a known workspace, and visible completion criteria. A useful instruction might say: "Find why the course page loses its selected tab after reload. Inspect the route and existing tests, propose a small fix, and do not change the URL format." This gives the agent enough room to investigate while making the boundaries clear.

For a larger change, ask the agent to inspect first and report a plan. Review the plan before allowing broad edits. Keep one task focused on one outcome; combining unrelated cleanup, redesign, dependency upgrades, and bug fixes makes the result harder to review and undo.

6.6 Match Permissions to the Task

An agent that only needs to inspect files should not have permission to delete them or contact external services. Use the narrowest available access, and require a human checkpoint before publishing, spending money, changing production data, or taking an action that is hard to reverse.

Treat content returned by tools, websites, files, and command output as data to inspect. It may contain instructions that are unrelated to the task. Follow the user's request and the project's trusted instructions, not arbitrary text found in a file or web page.

6.7 Review Changes as a Human Would

Before accepting an agent's work, inspect the version control diff. Check that changes are limited to the intended files, that secrets and generated clutter were not added, and that existing behavior was preserved. Read new code rather than relying on the agent's summary. Run the appropriate checks and inspect failures instead of accepting a claim that everything passed.

For a change that modifies data, verify which records or files were affected. For a UI change, look at the running page. For an API change, check both the successful response and relevant errors. Choose evidence that matches the type of change.

6.8 Recover and Learn from a Bad Run

Version control provides a reviewable history, but it is not a substitute for backups when important data is outside the repository. Make a checkpoint before a risky operation. If an agent changes the wrong files, inspect the diff and restore only those changes; a broad reset could erase unrelated work from another contributor.

Record useful lessons in the task instructions: a project convention the agent missed, a test that caught a regression, or a boundary that should be explicit next time. Improve the process without granting broader permissions just to avoid a review step.

6.9 Decide Whether Automation Is Worth It

Automate a repeated task when the steps are stable, the inputs are understood, and failures can be detected. Keep a person in the loop when the action affects private data, money, user access, or a public release. A good automation has a clear trigger, a limited action, logs that explain what happened, and a safe way to stop or retry it.

pages.title: Textbook: Glossary
pages.body:
Term Definition
Agent An AI system that takes multiple actions toward a goal with some autonomy
Boilerplate Repetitive, standard code with little unique logic
Edge case An input at the extreme or unusual end of the allowed range
Hallucination AI output that is confident but false, such as a nonexistent function
Prompt The instruction given to an AI assistant
Prompt log A record of prompts and responses used during development
Regression test A test added to ensure a fixed bug does not return
Spec A precise description of required behavior
Vibe coding Building software by directing an AI assistant in natural language

pages:
VIBE 101
Lecture 1: What Is Vibe Coding?
Dr. Quinn Ferrous

Textbook: Chapter 1

Today's Agenda
- Define vibe coding
- Where it shines, where it burns
- The Vibe Coding Loop
- Live demo: "Build me a to-do app" (what could go wrong?)

Definition
Vibe coding: building software by describing intent in natural language and having an AI generate most of the code.

Your job changes from typing to directing, reviewing, verifying.

Abstraction, Again
Machine code -> Assembly -> C -> Python -> Natural language

Key difference: compilers are deterministic. Language models are not.

> Same prompt, different code. Plan accordingly.

Where It Works
- Prototypes and throwaway scripts
- Boilerplate and config
- Learning new libraries
- Translating between languages
- First drafts of tests

Where It Struggles
- Big codebases with unwritten rules
- Safety- or performance-critical code
- Novel algorithms
- Anything where "mostly right" is not right

The Vibe Coding Loop
1. Describe
2. Generate
3. Read
4. Test
5. Refine

Steps 3 and 4 are not optional. They are the whole course.

Key Takeaway
You own the output.

"The AI wrote it" has the same legal and professional weight as "autocomplete wrote it."

Next time: Prompting as Specification

Lecture 2: Prompting as Specification
Textbook: Chapter 2

A Prompt Is a Spec
Weak: "Make a to-do app."

Strong: "Python CLI to-do app. Commands: add, done, list. JSON storage. IDs start at 1, never reused. Standard library only."

Which one would you want to implement?

Five Parts of a Good Prompt
1. Goal
2. Context
3. Constraints
4. Examples
5. Format

Examples Beat Adjectives
- [no] "Make it robust."
- [yes] "Return None for an empty list. Raise ValueError on negative values."

Edge cases in the prompt = fewer surprises in the code.

Iterating Without Spiraling
- Name what is wrong
- Change one thing at a time
- If you've rewritten the prompt 6 times, the spec is the problem

Prompt Logs
Record: prompt -> response -> what you changed and why.

Purpose: reproducibility, accountability, and grading. (Yes, we read them. Yes, all of them. Maya has opinions.)

Lecture 3: Reading Code You Didn't Write
Textbook: Chapter 3

The Reading Checklist
1. Matches the spec?
2. Trace by hand
3. Check boundaries
4. Check hidden assumptions
5. Check dependencies
6. Look for smells

Spot the Other Bug
def add_item(item, items=[]):
    items.append(item)
    return items
Call it twice. What do you get?

Answer: the default list is shared across calls. The second call returns both items.

Common AI Failure Modes
- Hallucinated APIs
- Plausible but wrong logic
- Silent except: pass
- Mutable default arguments
- Outdated practices
- Overengineering (a factory for a 10-line script)

Lecture 4: Tests First, Vibes Second
Textbook: Chapter 4

Tests Are the Seatbelt
"It seems to work" -> "It works on these cases."

Test-First Prompting
1. Write the spec
2. Write the tests
3. Generate code to pass them
4. Run the tests

(!) AI-written tests for AI-written code can share the same blind spots. Review both.

What to Test
- Normal cases
- Edge cases (empty, one, huge, duplicates)
- Error cases
- Regression cases (every fixed bug gets a test)

Systematic Debugging
1. Reproduce minimally
2. Locate the divergence
3. Hypothesize
4. Fix one thing
5. Re-run everything

Do not accept a "fix" that deletes the failing test.

Lecture 5: Security, Privacy, Ethics
Textbook: Chapter 5

Secrets
- Never paste keys into prompts
- Never commit them
- Use environment variables and .gitignore

API_KEY = "sk-12345"   # Delete this immediately

Vulnerabilities in Generated Code
- SQL injection (string-built queries)
- No input validation
- Insecure defaults (debug mode, weak hashing)
- Fake or malicious packages

Licensing, Privacy, Responsibility
- Generated code can resemble open-source code
- Don't send others' personal data to tools without permission
- You are accountable for what you ship

Lecture 6: Agents and Guardrails
Textbook: Chapter 6

Chat vs. Agent
Chat: answers questions.
Agent: takes multiple steps, edits files, runs commands.

More power. More ways to ruin your afternoon.

Guardrails
- Use version control
- Minimum permissions
- Approval for destructive actions
- Review every diff
- Human checkpoint before production

When Not to Vibe
- Security-critical code you must fully understand
- Concepts you are trying to learn
- High-stakes code where review costs more than writing

Course Wrap-Up
You can now:
- Write specs, not wishes
- Read before trusting
- Test before shipping
- Say "no" to the AI when needed

May your builds be green and your diffs be small.

assignments.name: Assignment 1: Hello, Vibes
assignments.description:
Assigned: Week 2 · Due: Week 4 · Points: 100 · Objectives: 1, 2, 6

Overview

Build a command-line to-do app in Python using an AI assistant, then document how you got there.

Requirements

The app must support:

  • add <text>: adds a task and prints its ID
  • done <id>: marks a task complete
  • list: prints all tasks as [ ] 1 Buy milk or [x] 1 Buy milk
  • Persistent storage in tasks.json
  • IDs are integers starting at 1 and are never reused, even after deletion
  • Standard library only

Deliverables

  1. todo.py
  2. README.md with usage instructions
  3. prompt_log.md with at least 5 prompts, including at least one where the first attempt was wrong and you corrected it
  4. reflection.md (200–300 words): What did the AI get right? What did you have to fix? What would you do differently in your first prompt?

General rules for all assignments

  • Submit your code, tests, and a prompt log (PDF or Markdown).
  • You may use any AI assistant. You must be able to explain every line.
  • Late policy: see syllabus.

rubric.description: Functionality: all commands work as specified
Edge cases: bad ID, empty list, missing/corrupt JSON handled
Code quality: readable, minimal, no dead code
Prompt log: honest, complete, shows iteration

assignments.name: Assignment 2: Spec First
assignments.description:
Assigned: Week 5 · Due: Week 7 · Points: 100 · Objectives: 2, 3, 4

Overview

Practice test-first development. You write the tests and spec before asking the AI for code.

Task

Implement a function normalize_scores(scores: list[float]) -> list[float] that scales a list of numbers to the range 0 to 1 using min-max normalization.

Steps

  1. Write a spec (1 page max) covering normal behavior and these cases: empty list, single element, all identical values, negative numbers, and non-numeric input.
  2. Write at least 8 unit tests (using pytest or unittest) before generating any code.
  3. Prompt an AI to implement the function. Include your spec in the prompt.
  4. Run your tests. For every failure, decide whether the code or the test is wrong, and explain.
  5. Add at least 2 regression tests for bugs you found along the way.

Deliverables

spec.md, test_normalize.py, normalize.py, prompt_log.md, failure_analysis.md

General rules for all assignments

  • Submit your code, tests, and a prompt log (PDF or Markdown).
  • You may use any AI assistant. You must be able to explain every line.
  • Late policy: see syllabus.

rubric.description: Spec: clear, complete, covers listed cases
Tests: meaningful, cover edge and error cases
Failure analysis: correct diagnosis of code vs. test errors

assignments.name: Assignment 3: The Bug Hunt
assignments.description:
Assigned: Week 9 · Due: Week 11 · Points: 100 · Objectives: 3, 4, 5

Overview

You are the code reviewer. The following AI-generated code was submitted by "an intern" for a small user-login helper. It has at least 6 problems spanning correctness, security, and style.

import sqlite3

users = []

def add_user(name, password, roles=[]):
    roles.append("user")
    conn = sqlite3.connect("app.db")
    conn.execute(
        "INSERT INTO users VALUES ('" + name + "', '" + password + "')"
    )
    conn.commit()
    return roles

def find_user(name):
    conn = sqlite3.connect("app.db")
    cur = conn.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name + "'")
    try:
        return cur.fetchone()
    except:
        pass

API_KEY = "sk-live-9f8e7d6c5b4a"

def average_age(ages):
    return sum(ages) / len(ages)

Tasks

  1. Find every problem. For each, give the line, the category (correctness, security, style), and why it matters.
  2. Rewrite the code to fix them.
  3. Write tests that would have caught at least 3 of the problems.
  4. Prompt an AI to review the original code. Compare its findings to yours. What did it miss? What did it catch that you missed?

Deliverables

review.md, fixed_users.py, test_users.py, ai_comparison.md

General rules for all assignments

  • Submit your code, tests, and a prompt log (PDF or Markdown).
  • You may use any AI assistant. You must be able to explain every line.
  • Late policy: see syllabus.

rubric.description: Issues found (up to 8 count): 5 pts each, with correct explanation
Fixed code is correct and secure

assignments.name: Final Project: Ship It
assignments.description:
Proposal: Week 12 · Due: Week 14 · Points: 100 · Objectives: all

Overview

Build and demo a small working application (web app, CLI, bot, or data tool) using AI assistance. Scope: roughly 10 hours of work. Smaller and finished beats bigger and broken.

Requirements

  • A working demo (5 minutes live)
  • Version-controlled repository with meaningful commits
  • At least 10 tests, passing
  • PROMPT_LOG.md and DECISIONS.md (3+ moments where you accepted, rejected, or modified AI output, and why)

General rules for all assignments

  • Late policy: see syllabus.

rubric.description: Demo and Q&A (can you explain your code?)

assignments.name: Quiz 1: Chapters 1–2
assignments.description:
Total: 20 points (8 MCQ × 2 pts, 2 short answer × 2 pts)

Multiple Choice

1. Which best defines vibe coding?

  • A. Writing code while listening to lo-fi music
  • B. Using an IDE with syntax highlighting
  • C. Letting an AI write and deploy code without human review
  • D. Building software by describing intent to an AI and directing, reviewing, and verifying its output

2. What is the key difference between a compiler and a language model?

  • A. Compilers are deterministic; language models are not
  • B. Language models cannot write Python
  • C. Compilers are faster
  • D. Compilers only work on small programs

3. Which task is generally a GOOD fit for vibe coding?

  • A. Flight-control software
  • B. A cryptographic library
  • C. A medical dosage calculator
  • D. A throwaway script to rename 200 files

4. In the Vibe Coding Loop, which steps are NOT optional?

  • A. Describe and Generate
  • B. Read and Test
  • C. Describe and Refine
  • D. Generate and Refine

5. Which prompt is the strongest?

  • A. "Write a Python function sort_desc(nums) that returns a new list sorted high to low, leaving the input unchanged. Example: [3,1,2] → [3,2,1]."
  • B. "Write a sorting function, make it fast and robust."
  • C. "Write a good sorting function."
  • D. "Write a sorting function."

6. The five parts of a good prompt are:

  • A. Input, Output, Process, Storage, Display
  • B. Who, What, When, Where, Why
  • C. Goal, Context, Constraints, Examples, Format
  • D. Goal, Tone, Length, Audience, Format

7. You've rewritten your prompt six times with small tweaks and still get wrong output. The most likely problem is:

  • A. You should switch programming languages
  • B. Your spec is unclear or incomplete
  • C. The model is broken
  • D. You need a longer prompt regardless of content

8. What is the purpose of a prompt log?

  • A. To satisfy the compiler
  • B. To record prompts, responses, and your changes so the process is documented and reproducible
  • C. To make the AI remember you
  • D. To increase code speed

Short Answer

9. Give one reason "the AI wrote it" is not an acceptable defense for a bug in production. (2 pts)

10. Rewrite this weak prompt into a stronger one: "Make a calculator." Include at least three of the five parts. (2 pts)

assignments.name: Quiz 2: Chapters 3–4
assignments.description:
Total: 20 points

Multiple Choice

1. What does this return on its second call?

def add(x, items=[]):
    items.append(x)
    return items
add(1); add(2)
  • A. [1, 2]
  • B. [1]
  • C. [2]
  • D. Error

2. What is a "hallucinated API"?

  • A. An API that responds slowly
  • B. An API with a graphical interface
  • C. A call to a function or library that does not exist
  • D. An undocumented but real endpoint

3. Which is the best first step when reviewing AI-generated code?

  • A. Ask the AI if it is correct
  • B. Delete the comments
  • C. Deploy it and see
  • D. Check whether it matches the spec and trace it on a small example

4. What is wrong with except: pass?

  • A. It is a syntax error
  • B. Nothing, it is best practice
  • C. It silently hides all errors, making failures hard to detect
  • D. It makes the code run slower

5. Which is an edge case for a function that finds the maximum of a list?

  • A. A list sorted in ascending order
  • B. A list of three positive numbers
  • C. A list of five numbers

6. In test-first prompting, you should:

  • A. Generate code, then write tests to match whatever it does
  • B. Write the spec and tests first, then have the AI generate code to pass them
  • C. Skip tests if the AI is confident
  • D. Only test error cases

7. Why can AI-written tests for AI-written code be risky?

  • A. They cannot run in pytest
  • B. They are not allowed in Python
  • C. They may share the same blind spots as the code
  • D. They are always too long

8. What is a regression test?

  • A. A test written in a statistical regression library
  • B. A test of the oldest code
  • C. A test added to ensure a previously fixed bug does not return
  • D. A test for slow code

Short Answer

9. Name two items from the six-item reading checklist and explain one in a sentence. (2 pts)

10. The assistant "fixed" your failing test by deleting the test. Explain what you should do instead. (2 pts)

assignments.name: Quiz 3: Chapter 5
assignments.description:
Total: 20 points

Multiple Choice

1. Where should an API key be stored?

assignments.name: Midterm Exam
assignments.description:
Closed notes, closed AI. You may use scratch paper. Write code by hand clearly; syntax mistakes will not be penalized if your intent is clear.

Time: 75 minutes · Total: 100 points Part I: 12 multiple choice × 3 pts = 36 · Part II: 3 free response = 64

Part I: Multiple Choice

1. What makes AI-generated code risky to trust without testing?

  • A. It always contains syntax errors
  • B. It is always slower than hand-written code
  • C. It can look plausible yet be wrong, and output varies between runs
  • D. It cannot use standard libraries

2. The spec says first(xs) returns None for an empty list. Which input exposes the bug in the code below?

def first(xs):
    return xs[0]
  • A. []
  • B. [1]
  • C. [1, 2, 3]
  • D. ["a"]

3. Which is the strongest rewrite of the prompt "Parse the dates"?

  • A. "Parse the dates better."
  • B. "Parse the dates quickly and robustly."
  • C. "Please parse the dates carefully."
  • D. "Write Python parse_date(s) that accepts 'YYYY-MM-DD' and returns a datetime.date; raise ValueError otherwise. Example: '2024-02-29' → date(2024, 2, 29)."

4. What does f(4) return?

def f(n):
    total = 0
    for i in range(1, n):
        total += i
    return total
  • A. 10
  • B. 6
  • C. 4
  • D. 3

5. The spec says f(n) should return the sum of the integers from 1 through n. Which change fixes the code in Question 4?

  • A. range(1, n + 1)
  • B. range(0, n)
  • C. range(1, n - 1)
  • D. range(n)

6. A regression test is:

  • A. A test that measures how fast code runs
  • B. A test for the oldest module in a project
  • C. A test added after fixing a bug to confirm it does not return
  • D. A test generated using regression analysis

7. A test fails. What should you do first?

  • A. Rewrite the function from scratch
  • B. Ask the AI to fix it and accept the answer
  • C. Add print statements everywhere
  • D. Reproduce the failure with the smallest possible input

8. An AI wrote both your tests and your code from the same ambiguous prompt, and all tests pass. The most accurate conclusion is:

  • A. The code is definitely correct
  • B. The tests show only that the code agrees with the tests, which may share the same misunderstanding
  • C. The tests are too short
  • D. The prompt must have been fine

9. The assistant's code has import fastjsonx, and you have never heard of it. The best action is:

  • A. Run pip install fastjsonx and see what happens
  • B. Ask the AI whether the package is real
  • C. Verify the package exists and is legitimate before installing anything
  • D. Rename the import to something familiar

10. Which is the strongest sign of overengineering?

  • A. An abstract factory and a config loader in a 10-line script
  • B. Meaningful variable names
  • C. A unit test
  • D. A docstring

11. Which best describes the programmer's role in vibe coding?

  • A. Typing every line by hand
  • B. Waiting for the AI to finish
  • C. Choosing the programming language only
  • D. Directing, reviewing, and verifying the AI's output

12. What does this code print?

def g(acc=[]):
    acc.append(len(acc))
    return acc

g()
print(g())
  • A. [1]
  • B. [0, 1]
  • C. [0]
  • D. [1, 1]

Part II: Free Response

FRQ 1 (20 pts): Prompts as Specs. A teammate writes this prompt: "Write a function that cleans up a list of names." (a) (10 pts) Rewrite the prompt so that it includes all five parts of a good prompt (goal, context, constraints, examples, format). Label each part. (b) (6 pts) List three edge cases the new prompt should address. (c) (4 pts) Explain in 1–2 sentences why examples help more than adjectives like "robust."

FRQ 2 (24 pts): Review and Repair. The spec: top_n(scores, n) returns the n highest scores in descending order, does not modify the input list, returns all scores if n exceeds the list length, and returns [] if n <= 0.

def top_n(scores, n):
    scores.sort()
    return scores[:n]

(a) (9 pts) Identify at least three ways this code violates the spec. (b) (7 pts) Write a corrected version. (c) (8 pts) Write at least four unit tests (as assert statements) that would catch the bugs. Include at least two edge cases.

FRQ 3 (20 pts): Argue It. A teammate says, "We don't need to write tests. The AI is really good now." In 150–200 words, respond. Your answer must (i) give at least two specific reasons tests are still necessary, (ii) mention one limitation of AI-written tests, and (iii) suggest a practical workflow.

assignments.name: Final Exam
assignments.description:
Closed notes, closed AI. You may use scratch paper. Write code by hand clearly; syntax mistakes will not be penalized if your intent is clear.

Time: 110 minutes · Total: 100 points Part I: 10 multiple choice × 3 pts = 30 · Part II: 2 free response × 35 = 70

Part I: Multiple Choice

1. What distinguishes an agent from a basic chat assistant?

  • A. It never makes mistakes
  • B. It takes multiple steps toward a goal with some autonomy, such as editing files or running commands
  • C. It runs only on local machines
  • D. It cannot use tools

2. Which is the best safeguard before letting an agent modify your codebase?

  • A. Disable all tests to avoid conflicts
  • B. Give it administrator access so it never gets blocked
  • C. Trust that it will ask if it's unsure
  • D. Work in a version-controlled repository and review the diff before accepting changes

3. You discover an API key committed to a public repository. Your first action should be to:

  • A. Revoke or rotate the key immediately
  • B. Delete the commit and assume the problem is solved
  • C. Wait to see whether anyone uses it
  • D. Change the variable name

4. Which code is safe from SQL injection?

  • A. db.execute("SELECT * FROM t WHERE n='" + name + "'")
  • B. db.execute(f"SELECT * FROM t WHERE n='{name}'")
  • C. db.execute("SELECT * FROM t WHERE n = ?", (name,))
  • D. db.execute("SELECT * FROM t WHERE n=" + repr(name))

5. Which test best targets a boundary case for mean(xs) defined as sum(xs) / len(xs)?

  • A. mean([1, 2, 3])
  • B. mean([5, 5, 5])
  • C. mean([10, 20])
  • D. mean([])

6. When is it most appropriate to write code by hand rather than using AI?

  • A. Boilerplate configuration files
  • B. A throwaway script
  • C. Learning a new concept you are trying to master, or security-critical code you must fully understand
  • D. Translating a short function between languages

7. Which is a privacy concern when using AI coding tools?

  • A. Using meaningful variable names
  • B. Pasting real user records into a third-party tool without permission
  • C. Writing unit tests
  • D. Adding comments

8. An agent proposes running rm -rf on a project directory. The best policy is:

  • A. Require explicit human approval for destructive or irreversible actions
  • B. Let it proceed to save time
  • C. Allow it only on weekends
  • D. Ask the agent whether it is sure, then proceed if it says yes

9. After an AI "fix," your failing test now passes, but you notice the test file no longer contains that test. What should you do?

  • A. Accept the fix, since the suite is green
  • B. Ask the AI to rewrite the test
  • C. Delete the other tests too for consistency
  • D. Restore the test and require the code, not the test, to be changed to pass

10. Which statement is most accurate?

  • A. AI assistance eliminates the need for code review
  • B. AI-generated code is always insecure
  • C. AI assistance changes where effort goes, but verification is still required
  • D. Only beginners benefit from AI assistance

Part II: Free Response

FRQ 1 (35 pts): Security Review.

import sqlite3

SECRET = "hunter2-prod"

def login(name, pw):
    db = sqlite3.connect("app.db")
    q = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name='{name}' AND pw='{pw}'"
    return db.execute(q).fetchone() is not None

(a) (10 pts) Identify at least three security or quality problems and explain why each matters. (b) (15 pts) Rewrite login to fix them. You may assume a helper verify_password(pw, stored_hash) exists. (c) (10 pts) Write two tests that would catch problems in the original.

FRQ 2 (35 pts): Agent Guardrails. Your team plans to let an AI agent make multi-file changes and run shell commands in your project. (a) (16 pts) Propose a guardrail plan with at least four distinct safeguards. For each, explain the specific risk it addresses. (b) (9 pts) Describe one situation where you would choose not to use an agent and justify your choice. (c) (10 pts) Explain how your prompt log and a DECISIONS.md file support accountability when something goes wrong.

submission_comments.comment:
Jordan, nice work. Your code is short, readable, and it runs, which is already more than some "enterprise" software can claim. The reflection was the highlight of this submission. You wrote that your biggest mistake was "asking for features instead of describing rules," and that is exactly the lesson of Chapter 2.

Two things to address:

1. IDs are reused. `new_id = len(tasks) + 1` means that if you delete task 2 of 3, the next task gets ID 3 and collides with the existing one. The spec said IDs are never reused, which implies you need to track a `next_id` separately or use `max(id) + 1`. submission_comments.comment:
Marcus, you have the core ideas right. You noticed the mutation and the wrong sort order, and your `copy()` plus `reverse=True` fix is clean and readable. Many students missed the mutation bug entirely, so well done.

Where points were lost:

1. The `n <= 0` requirement. The spec explicitly says "returns `[]` if `n <= 0`." With your code, `top_n([1,2,3], -1)` returns `[3, 2]` because `s[:-1]` means "everything except the last item." That is a classic slicing trap, and it is the sort of subtle behavior AI-generated code gets wrong while sounding confident. Adding `max(n, 0)` fixes it.
2. Your tests are all happy-path. The question asked for at least two edge cases. Edge cases are where bugs live: `n = 0`, `n = -1`, an empty list, and duplicates are all good candidates. Notice that if you had written a test for `n = -1`, you would have discovered your own bug in part (b). This is exactly why we write tests before the code.
3. You did not test that the input list is unchanged, which was one of the three spec requirements. A test like `s = [3,1,2]; top_n(s, 2); assert s == [3,1,2]` would have covered it.

Next step: For every function you write this term, make a list titled "ways this could break" before you write any code. Five minutes of pessimism saves an hour of debugging.

Elena, solid exam. Part (b) was the best answer I read. You gave a specific situation, and you tied your reasoning to verification cost, which is exactly the argument from Chapter 6.

Two notes for improvement:

- Part (a): safeguards without risks. The question asked you to explain "the specific risk it addresses." You listed the safeguards, which are all correct, but you lost 4 points because you did not say what could go wrong without them. For instance: "Require approval before delete commands, because an agent running `rm -rf` on the wrong directory could cause irreversible data loss." The safeguard shows you know the tool. The risk shows you understand why it exists.
- Part (c): make it concrete. "The prompt log shows what happened" is true but general. A stronger answer: "If production broke after an agent change, the prompt log tells me which instruction triggered it, and DECISIONS.md tells me whether we accepted the agent's output deliberately or by accident." One example turns a definition into an argument.

Next step: In any future design doc, practice the "safeguard → risk" pattern. It is the difference between a checklist and a justification.
